title: Mesothelioma - Asbestos Exposure and Palliative Care

patient_demographics.name: George Patterson
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: Progressive breathlessness and right-sided chest pain for 3 months

scenario: Mr Patterson is a 72-year-old retired construction worker presenting to the respiratory clinic at Liverpool Hospital with progressive dyspnoea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He worked in asbestos removal and shipbuilding at Garden Island Naval Base from 1970-1985 without protective equipment. His CT chest shows right pleural thickening with nodularity and moderate pleural effusion. Thoracoscopic biopsy confirmed epithelioid mesothelioma. He lives with his wife and has two adult children. Performance status ECOG 2.

history.presenting_complaint: Worsening breathlessness over 3 months with right chest pain, worse on deep breathing. Unable to walk 50 metres without stopping. Night sweats and 8kg weight loss. Dry cough, no haemoptysis.
history.occupational_history: Asbestos exposure 1970-1985 at Garden Island Naval Base and Cockatoo Island Dockyard. Direct handling of asbestos lagging on ships' pipes. No respiratory protection provided. Witnessed many colleagues develop asbestos-related diseases.
history.past_medical_history: Pleural plaques noted on chest X-ray 2015. Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Hypertension. Osteoarthritis.
history.medications: Metformin 1000mg BD (PBS code: 8435N). Perindopril 5mg daily (PBS code: 8532Y). Paracetamol 1g QID PRN.
history.social_history: Ex-smoker, quit 2005 (40 pack-years). Lives with wife in Fairfield. Two adult children, four grandchildren. Previously very active, now housebound. Eligible for Dust Diseases Board compensation.
history.family_history: Father died lung cancer age 68 (also worked in shipbuilding). Mother died CVA age 82.

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 91% on room air, 95% on 2L nasal prongs

physical_examination.general_appearance: Cachectic elderly man, breathless at rest, using accessory muscles. Sitting upright, unable to lie flat.
physical_examination.cardiovascular: JVP elevated 4cm. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs. Peripheral oedema absent.
physical_examination.respiratory: Reduced chest expansion right side. Trachea central. Percussion stony dull right base to mid-zone. Reduced breath sounds right hemithorax. No wheeze or crackles. Vocal resonance decreased right side.
physical_examination.abdominal: Soft, non-tender. No organomegaly or masses. No ascites.
physical_examination.neurological: Alert and oriented. No focal deficits. Power 5/5 all limbs.
physical_examination.other: Clubbing grade 2. No lymphadenopathy. Thoracoscopy port sites healed.

imaging.chest_xray: Large right pleural effusion with pleural thickening. Mediastinal shift to left. No pneumothorax.
imaging.ct_chest: Circumferential right pleural thickening up to 18mm. Nodular pleural disease. Moderate-large right pleural effusion. Volume loss right lung. No contralateral disease. Mediastinal nodes 12mm.
imaging.pet_ct: FDG-avid right pleural disease SUVmax 8.2. No distant metastases.

pleural_fluid.cytology: Atypical mesothelial cells consistent with mesothelioma

investigations.histopathology: Video-assisted thoracoscopic biopsy: Epithelioid mesothelioma, calretinin and WT1 positive, TTF-1 and CEA negative
investigations.lung_function: FEV1 1.4L (48% predicted), FVC 1.8L (45% predicted), FEV1/FVC 78%, DLCO 42% predicted

diagnosis: Malignant pleural mesothelioma (epithelioid subtype), Stage IIIB (T4N0M0), secondary to occupational asbestos exposure

immediate: Indwelling pleural catheter insertion for symptom control
Oxygen therapy titrated to maintain SpO2 >92%
Oxycodone SR 10mg BD (PBS code: 5467K) for pain control
Referral to palliative care team at Liverpool Hospital
chemotherapy: Pre-chemotherapy assessment: renal function, hearing, cardiac function
Folic acid 5mg daily and vitamin B12 supplementation if proceeding
supportive_care: Dust Diseases Board claim assistance - eligible for compensation
Social work for advance care planning and family support
Psychology referral for adjustment to diagnosis
monitoring: Weekly pleural drainage via indwelling catheter
Monthly clinical review with chest X-ray
Symptom assessment using modified Borg dyspnoea scale
management_plan.prognosis_discussion: Median survival 12-18 months with epithelioid subtype. Discuss goals of care, advance care directives, and preferred place of death

key_clinical_points: Mesothelioma has 20-40 year latency from asbestos exposure
Australia has highest per capita incidence due to historical asbestos use
Epithelioid subtype has better prognosis than sarcomatoid
Immunohistochemistry essential for diagnosis (calretinin, WT1, CK5/6 positive)
Dust Diseases Board provides compensation for asbestos-related diseases in NSW
Indwelling pleural catheter preferred over repeated thoracentesis
Palliative radiotherapy may help with pain control
Consider trial eligibility (CheckMate 743 - ipilimumab/nivolumab)
marking_criteria: Takes comprehensive occupational history including specific asbestos exposure details and timeline
Correctly identifies clinical signs of pleural effusion (dullness, reduced breath sounds, decreased vocal resonance)
Explains mesothelioma diagnosis with appropriate sensitivity and clarity
Discusses prognosis honestly while maintaining hope and focusing on symptom control
Arranges indwelling pleural catheter for symptom management
Initiates appropriate analgesia following WHO pain ladder
Makes timely referral to palliative care services
Addresses Dust Diseases Board compensation eligibility
Involves family in discussions with patient consent
Documents advance care planning discussions
Considers chemotherapy eligibility based on performance status
Arranges multidisciplinary team input (oncology, palliative care, social work)

title: Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP) - Steroid Treatment

patient_demographics.name: Margaret Chen
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: Persistent cough and breathlessness for 8 weeks

scenario: Mrs Chen is a 58-year-old primary school teacher presenting to the respiratory outpatient clinic at Royal North Shore Hospital with 8 weeks of non-resolving cough, progressive dyspnoea, and fatigue. She was treated with two courses of antibiotics by her GP without improvement. HRCT chest shows bilateral patchy consolidation with peribronchovascular distribution and ground-glass opacities. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy confirms organizing pneumonia with no identifiable cause. She has never smoked and has no significant occupational exposures.

history.presenting_complaint: Dry cough for 8 weeks, initially thought to be post-viral. Progressive breathlessness on exertion - can only climb one flight of stairs. Fatigue and malaise. Low-grade fevers to 37.8°C. No chest pain or haemoptysis. Lost 3kg weight.
history.treatment_history: Amoxicillin 500mg TDS for 7 days - no improvement. Doxycycline 100mg BD for 7 days - no improvement. Ventolin inhaler - minimal benefit.
history.past_medical_history: Hypothyroidism. Osteoporosis. GORD. No previous respiratory disease.
history.medications: Levothyroxine 100mcg daily (PBS code: 2182F). Alendronate 70mg weekly (PBS code: 8255K). Esomeprazole 20mg daily (PBS code: 8535B). Calcium/Vitamin D supplement.
history.social_history: Never smoker. No alcohol. Teacher at Chatswood Primary School for 20 years. Lives with husband. Two adult children. No pets. No recent travel.
history.family_history: Mother - rheumatoid arthritis. Father - Type 2 diabetes. No lung disease.

physical_examination.general_appearance: Alert, mildly dyspnoeic on talking. No cyanosis or clubbing.
physical_examination.cardiovascular: Heart sounds dual, no murmurs. JVP not elevated. No peripheral oedema.
physical_examination.respiratory: Bilateral fine inspiratory crackles in mid and lower zones. No wheeze. Normal percussion note. Chest expansion symmetrical but reduced.
physical_examination.musculoskeletal: No joint swelling or deformity. No muscle weakness.

blood_tests.fbc: Hb 118 g/L (115-165), WCC 12.8 x10^9/L (4-11), Neutrophils 9.2 x10^9/L, Eosinophils 0.3 x10^9/L
blood_tests.biochemistry: Normal electrolytes, renal and liver function
blood_tests.autoimmune: ANA negative, ANCA negative, RF negative, Anti-CCP negative, Anti-Jo-1 negative

imaging.chest_xray: Bilateral patchy alveolar opacities, predominantly peripheral and basal distribution
imaging.hrct_chest: Bilateral patchy consolidation with air bronchograms. Ground-glass opacities. Peribronchovascular distribution. Subpleural sparing. No honeycombing or traction bronchiectasis. No lymphadenopathy.

bronchoscopy.bal: Total cell count increased. Lymphocytes 28%, Neutrophils 45%, Eosinophils 3%, Macrophages 24%. No malignant cells. No organisms on culture.
bronchoscopy.transbronchial_biopsy: Organizing pneumonia pattern with Masson bodies in alveolar ducts and alveoli. No granulomas, vasculitis, or malignancy. No viral inclusions.

investigations.lung_function: FEV1 1.8L (75% predicted), FVC 2.1L (72% predicted), FEV1/FVC 86%, DLCO 58% predicted
investigations.six_minute_walk: Distance 320m (65% predicted), desaturation to 88% on room air

diagnosis: Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP) - idiopathic form with typical clinical-radiological-pathological features

supportive_care: Supplemental oxygen PRN to maintain SpO2 >92%
steroid_monitoring: Baseline DEXA scan given osteoporosis history
Continue alendronate 70mg weekly with calcium/vitamin D
Consider PCP prophylaxis if prolonged high-dose steroids (Bactrim DS 160/800mg MWF)
disease_monitoring: Clinical review in 4 weeks - expect improvement in symptoms
relapse_prevention: Slow steroid taper essential - rapid taper associated with relapse
If relapse occurs, restart at previous effective dose
Consider steroid-sparing agent if frequent relapses (azathioprine, mycophenolate)

key_clinical_points: COP presents with subacute respiratory symptoms (weeks to months)
Typical HRCT pattern: patchy consolidation with air bronchograms, GGO, peribronchovascular distribution
Must exclude secondary causes (drugs, connective tissue disease, infection, malignancy)
Transbronchial biopsy showing organizing pneumonia with Masson bodies confirms diagnosis
Excellent response to corticosteroids in 65-80% of cases
Relapse rate 13-58%, usually during steroid taper
Minimum treatment duration 6 months, often 12 months
Monitor for steroid side effects especially with osteoporosis history
Alternative diagnoses: CEP, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, NSIP
Poor prognostic factors: hypoxaemia, extent of infiltrates on HRCT
marking_criteria: Recognises organizing pneumonia pattern on HRCT (consolidation, GGO, peribronchovascular distribution)
Systematically excludes secondary causes of OP (drugs, CTD, infection)
Correctly interprets bronchoscopy findings confirming organizing pneumonia
Initiates appropriate dose of prednisolone (0.5-1mg/kg/day)
Plans appropriate duration of treatment (minimum 6 months)
Implements slow steroid taper to prevent relapse
Addresses steroid-related complications (osteoporosis protection, glucose monitoring)
Arranges appropriate follow-up imaging and lung function testing
Counsels patient about expected treatment response (improvement within 2-4 weeks)
Discusses relapse risk and monitoring
Considers PCP prophylaxis for prolonged high-dose steroids
Documents clear tapering schedule for steroids

title: Pulmonary Embolism in Pregnancy - Anticoagulation Management

patient_demographics.name: Sarah Mitchell
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: Sudden onset chest pain and breathlessness at 28 weeks gestation

scenario: Mrs Mitchell is a 32-year-old marketing manager, G2P1 at 28 weeks gestation, presenting to the Emergency Department at Royal Prince Alfred Hospital with sudden onset pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea that started 3 hours ago. She has no significant past medical history but her mother had a DVT during pregnancy. CTPA confirms segmental pulmonary emboli in the right lower lobe. She is haemodynamically stable. The obstetric team has been notified.

history.presenting_complaint: Sudden sharp right-sided chest pain 3 hours ago, worse on deep breathing. Associated breathlessness and feeling faint. No haemoptysis. Mild right calf discomfort for 2 days. No fever or productive cough.
history.obstetric_history: G2P1. Currently 28+3 weeks. First pregnancy uncomplicated vaginal delivery 3 years ago. Current pregnancy: normal morphology scan, GDM screen negative. Regular antenatal care at RPAH.
history.past_medical_history: Nil significant. No previous VTE. No known thrombophilia.
history.medications: Elevit pregnancy multivitamin. Iron supplement 325mg daily.
history.social_history: Never smoker. No alcohol in pregnancy. Works from home since COVID. Lives with husband. Good support.
history.family_history: Mother - DVT during pregnancy age 28, on warfarin briefly. Maternal grandmother - PE age 65. No known thrombophilia testing in family.

physical_examination.general_appearance: Anxious, tachypnoeic pregnant woman. No cyanosis.
physical_examination.cardiovascular: Tachycardic, regular rhythm. Heart sounds normal. Loud P2. No murmurs. Right calf slightly swollen, tender.
physical_examination.respiratory: Clear breath sounds bilaterally. No wheeze or crackles. Reduced air entry right base.
physical_examination.obstetric: Gravid uterus consistent with dates. Fetal movements present. FHR 145bpm on CTG, reactive trace.
physical_examination.legs: Right calf circumference 38cm, left 36cm. Right calf tender. Positive Homan's sign right.

blood_tests.fbc: Hb 108 g/L (pregnancy range 105-140), WCC 11.2 x10^9/L, Platelets 185 x10^9/L
blood_tests.arterial_blood_gas: pH 7.44, PaO2 78mmHg on room air, PaCO2 32mmHg, HCO3 22mmol/L

imaging.chest_xray: No consolidation or pleural effusion. Mild elevation right hemidiaphragm
imaging.ctpa: Filling defects in segmental branches of right lower lobe pulmonary artery. No right heart strain. No pleural effusion
imaging.venous_doppler_legs: Acute DVT in right popliteal and posterior tibial veins

investigations.ecg: Sinus tachycardia 110bpm. S1Q3T3 pattern. Incomplete RBBB

diagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism with associated right leg DVT at 28 weeks gestation. Intermediate-low risk PE (no right heart strain, haemodynamically stable)

immediate: Initial dose: 80mg BD (based on current pregnant weight 78kg)
First dose given in ED after diagnosis confirmed
anticoagulation_pregnancy: Anti-Xa level 4 hours post-dose on day 3 (target 0.6-1.0 IU/mL)
Adjust dose if needed based on anti-Xa levels
Check anti-Xa monthly and with significant weight change
delivery_planning: Plan for 37-38 weeks induction if stable
Stop enoxaparin when labour established or 24 hours before planned induction
Epidural safe 12 hours after prophylactic dose, 24 hours after therapeutic dose
Consider IV heparin infusion if delivery <24 hours from last LMWH
postpartum_anticoagulation: Restart enoxaparin 6-12 hours post-vaginal delivery, 12-24 hours post-caesarean
Continue therapeutic anticoagulation for minimum 6 weeks postpartum
Total minimum duration 3 months from VTE diagnosis
Can transition to warfarin postpartum if preferred (safe with breastfeeding)
thrombophilia_screening: Defer testing until 6 weeks post-completion of anticoagulation
Screen for: Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin gene mutation, Antithrombin deficiency
monitoring: Growth scans given VTE in pregnancy
Platelet count weekly for first 2 weeks (HIT screening)
Educate about signs of bleeding, recurrent VTE

key_clinical_points: VTE risk increased 5-fold in pregnancy, highest postpartum period
CTPA preferred over V/Q in pregnancy for PE diagnosis (lower fetal radiation)
D-dimer physiologically elevated in pregnancy - limited diagnostic value
LMWH preferred over UFH (better bioavailability, less HIT risk)
Therapeutic dose enoxaparin 1mg/kg BD (not 1.5mg/kg daily in pregnancy)
Anti-Xa monitoring recommended in pregnancy (altered pharmacokinetics)
Warfarin contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic first trimester, bleeding risk third)
Timing of neuraxial anaesthesia critical - coordinate with anaesthetics
Postpartum anticoagulation essential - highest risk period
Future pregnancies will require thromboprophylaxis
marking_criteria: Recognises clinical features suggestive of PE in pregnancy
Appropriately investigates with CTPA (not V/Q scan initially)
Identifies concurrent DVT on examination and investigation
Initiates therapeutic anticoagulation promptly with LMWH
Calculates correct enoxaparin dose based on current pregnant weight
Plans anti-Xa monitoring (pregnancy-specific target range)
Involves multidisciplinary team (obstetrics, haematology, anaesthetics)
Develops clear delivery plan regarding anticoagulation management
Addresses epidural timing and safety with LMWH
Plans appropriate duration of postpartum anticoagulation
Defers thrombophilia testing until after anticoagulation completed
Counsels about future pregnancy risk and need for prophylaxis
Documents clear plan for anticoagulation peripartum

title: Tracheal Stenosis - Post-Intubation Complication

patient_demographics.name: Robert Anderson
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: Progressive difficulty breathing and stridor for 6 weeks

scenario: Mr Anderson is a 45-year-old electrician presenting to the respiratory clinic at Prince of Wales Hospital with progressive dyspnoea and audible wheeze for 6 weeks. He was intubated for 12 days with COVID-19 pneumonia 3 months ago at St Vincent's Hospital. He initially recovered well but has developed worsening breathlessness and noisy breathing. His GP treated him for asthma without improvement. Flexible bronchoscopy shows 70% concentric tracheal stenosis 3cm below the vocal cords.

history.presenting_complaint: Progressive breathlessness over 6 weeks. Initially on exertion, now at rest. High-pitched noisy breathing audible to others. Voice slightly hoarse. Unable to work due to symptoms. Worse when lying flat.
history.covid_history: Severe COVID-19 pneumonia 3 months ago. Intubated day 3 of admission. Ventilated for 12 days. Tracheostomy not required. ICU stay 16 days total. Required proning and neuromuscular blockade.
history.past_medical_history: No previous respiratory disease. Hypertension. Obesity.
history.medications: Symbicort 200/6 2 puffs BD (started by GP, PBS code: 8962L). Ventolin PRN. Perindopril 10mg daily. Atorvastatin 40mg nocte.
history.social_history: Current smoker 10 cigarettes/day (20 pack-years). Lives with partner. Self-employed electrician. Unable to work past 6 weeks.

physical_examination.general_appearance: Audible biphasic stridor at rest. Using accessory muscles. Anxious.
physical_examination.respiratory: Stridor loudest over trachea. Transmitted upper airway sounds throughout chest. No focal chest signs.
physical_examination.neck: No palpable masses or lymphadenopathy. Trachea central. No surgical scars.

lung_function.flow_volume_loop: Fixed upper airway obstruction pattern - plateau of inspiratory and expiratory limbs

imaging.chest_xray: Normal lung fields. Tracheal narrowing visible on lateral view
imaging.ct_neck_chest: Concentric tracheal stenosis extending 2cm, starting 3cm below vocal cords. Minimum diameter 6mm (normal 15-20mm). No mediastinal masses

bronchoscopy.flexible: Vocal cords normal. Concentric web-like stenosis 3cm below cords. Estimated 70% stenosis. Unable to pass standard bronchoscope. Mucosa inflamed but no granulation tissue

diagnosis: Post-intubation tracheal stenosis (PITS) - Cotton-Myer Grade III, subglottic location, 2cm length

immediate: Heliox (70% helium/30% oxygen) if respiratory distress
Monitor for deterioration - may need urgent intervention
definitive_treatment: Refer to interventional pulmonology/ENT at Prince of Wales
1. Bronchoscopic dilatation - temporary measure, likely to recur
2. Laser therapy with dilatation - for short segment stenosis
3. Tracheal resection and end-to-end anastomosis - definitive for stenosis <4cm
Patient likely candidate for resection given 2cm length
surgical_planning: Rigid bronchoscopy under GA for precise assessment
May need initial dilatation if symptomatic while awaiting surgery
Tracheal resection via cervical approach likely
Post-operative: Chin-to-chest sutures for 7 days to reduce tension
alternative_if_not_surgical_candidate: Consider tracheal stent as last resort (high complication rate)
follow_up: Urgent ENT/thoracic surgery review within 1 week
Serial flow-volume loops to monitor progression

key_clinical_points: PITS typically presents 2-3 months after extubation
Risk factors: prolonged intubation >7 days, traumatic intubation, oversized ETT, high cuff pressure
Biphasic stridor indicates severe stenosis >50%
Flow-volume loop shows fixed upper airway obstruction pattern
Often misdiagnosed as asthma - poor response to bronchodilators is key
Cotton-Myer grading: Grade I <50%, Grade II 51-70%, Grade III 71-99%, Grade IV no lumen
Tracheal resection gold standard for stenosis <4cm in suitable candidates
Success rate of resection >95% in experienced centres
Bronchoscopic management has high recurrence rate but useful as bridge
Smoking cessation crucial for surgical success
marking_criteria: Recognises stridor as sign of upper airway obstruction not asthma
Identifies post-intubation period as risk factor for tracheal stenosis
Correctly interprets flow-volume loop showing fixed obstruction
Stops inappropriate asthma therapy
Arranges urgent bronchoscopy for diagnosis and grading
Refers appropriately to ENT/thoracic surgery
Discusses treatment options including surgical and bronchoscopic
Addresses smoking cessation as priority before surgery
Recognises potential for acute deterioration and makes safety plan
Uses CT imaging to assess length and location of stenosis
Explains diagnosis and natural history to patient
Documents Cotton-Myer grade and stenosis characteristics

title: Hypoxic-Ischaemic Encephalopathy Post-Cardiac Arrest - Ventilator Weaning
scenario: Mr Thompson is a 52-year-old bank manager who suffered an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest 3 weeks ago due to anterior STEMI. He received bystander CPR for 8 minutes before ROSC. He underwent primary PCI and therapeutic hypothermia. MRI brain shows moderate hypoxic-ischaemic injury affecting basal ganglia and watershed zones. He has been difficult to wean from ventilation in ICU at Westmead Hospital. He is now tracheostomised and on pressure support ventilation. Neurology suggests poor prognosis for meaningful recovery. The family is struggling with decisions about ongoing care.

history.cardiac_arrest_details: Witnessed collapse at home 3 weeks ago. Wife performed CPR immediately. Ambulance arrived 8 minutes later. Initial rhythm VF. ROSC after 15 minutes total. Anterior STEMI on ECG. Primary PCI to LAD within 90 minutes.
history.icu_course: Therapeutic hypothermia 33°C for 24 hours. Initially comatose, GCS 3. Myoclonic jerks day 2-4. Started on levetiracetam. Percutaneous tracheostomy day 10. Multiple failed spontaneous breathing trials. Currently GCS 7 (E2, V1-trache, M4).
history.neurological_status: MRI brain day 7: Bilateral basal ganglia T2 hyperintensity, watershed infarcts, diffuse cerebral oedema resolved. EEG: Diffuse slowing, no epileptiform activity. Neurology opinion: Severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, poor prognosis for meaningful recovery.
history.medications: Aspirin 100mg daily. Ticagrelor 90mg BD. Atorvastatin 80mg. Bisoprolol 5mg. Ramipril 10mg. Levetiracetam 1000mg BD. Morphine infusion 2mg/hr. Midazolam 2mg/hr PRN.
history.social_history: Married, two teenage children. Previously independent, working full-time. Wife is primary decision-maker.
history.family_discussions: Wife hoping for recovery. Children distressed. No advance care directive. Previously expressed wish not to be kept alive on machines if no hope of recovery.

physical_examination.neurological: GCS 7 (E2 to pain, V1-trache, M4 withdraws to pain). Pupils 3mm equal and reactive. Positive corneal reflexes. Positive gag reflex. Intermittent spontaneous eye opening. No purposeful movements. Increased tone all limbs. Brisk reflexes. Bilateral Babinski positive.
physical_examination.respiratory: Tracheostomy in situ. On PSV: PS 10, PEEP 5, FiO2 0.35. Weak cough effort. Moderate secretions. Bilateral basal crackles.
physical_examination.cardiovascular: Stable haemodynamics. Heart sounds normal. No murmurs. Well-healed PCI access site.
physical_examination.gastrointestinal: PEG tube in situ. Tolerating feeds 60mL/hr. Bowels open with aperients.

current_ventilation.rsbi: 85 (RR/VT in litres) - borderline for weaning success

weaning_assessments.sbt_attempts: Failed 3 spontaneous breathing trials - tachypnoea and distress after 20 minutes

blood_tests.biochemistry: Na 138, K 4.1, Cr 78, Urea 5.2, Albumin 28 g/L

imaging.chest_xray: Bilateral lower zone atelectasis. No consolidation. Tracheostomy and PEG in situ
imaging.ct_brain: Established hypoxic-ischaemic changes basal ganglia and watershed zones. No hydrocephalus

neurophysiology.ssep: Absent N20 responses bilaterally (poor prognostic sign)
neurophysiology.neuron_specific_enolase: 85 μg/L at 72 hours (>33 suggests poor outcome)

diagnosis: Severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy with ventilator dependence post-cardiac arrest. Failed ventilator weaning due to combination of neurological impairment and respiratory muscle weakness

immediate_respiratory: Daily spontaneous breathing trials when ready
Aggressive secretion management - chest physiotherapy QID
Consider speaking valve trials to assess upper airway patency
prognostication: Poor prognostic indicators: Absent SSEP N20, elevated NSE, MRI changes
Arrange family meeting with ICU, neurology, palliative care
family_meeting_agenda: Discuss discordance between previously expressed wishes and current situation
Options: 1) Continue current care, 2) Comfort care pathway, 3) Chronic ventilation facility
Offer spiritual care and psychology support
if_continuing_active_treatment: Transfer to respiratory HDU for weaning program
Intensive rehabilitation with physiotherapy, OT, speech
Serial neurological assessments for any improvement
if_transitioning_to_comfort_care: Symptom management plan for terminal wean
Allow family presence, remove monitors if desired
chronic_ventilation_option: Refer to chronic ventilation facility (e.g., Sacred Heart Hospice)
Home ventilation unlikely given neurological status
Ongoing medical review and family support

key_clinical_points: Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy severity correlates with arrest duration and CPR quality
Multi-modal prognostication at 72+ hours: clinical exam, EEG, SSEP, biomarkers, MRI
Absent SSEP N20 responses highly specific for poor outcome
NSE >33 μg/L at 48-72 hours suggests poor prognosis
Ventilator dependence may be due to central drive failure, not just weakness
CPC (Cerebral Performance Category): 1-2 good outcome, 3-5 poor outcome
Family meetings require sensitivity, clear communication, and time
Comfort care pathway requires careful symptom management
Chronic ventilation facilities limited in Australia
Moral distress common in ICU staff with poor prognosis cases
Consider organ donation discussion if transitioning to end-of-life care
marking_criteria: Accurately assesses neurological status and prognosis using multi-modal approach
Recognises poor prognostic indicators (absent SSEP, elevated NSE, MRI changes)
Attempts appropriate ventilator weaning strategies
Identifies combination of central and peripheral factors preventing weaning
Arranges multidisciplinary family meeting with appropriate teams
Discusses all options sensitively: continue care, comfort pathway, chronic ventilation
Addresses discordance between previously expressed wishes and current care
Develops clear comfort care protocol if family chooses this pathway
Provides appropriate psychological support to family
Documents discussions clearly including family understanding
Considers referral to chronic ventilation facility if appropriate
Manages moral distress in healthcare team
Addresses practical aspects (PEG feeding, secretion management, DVT prophylaxis)
